title: (Scenario) How would you scale a key-value store toward ~1M requests/sec — why is "add more servers" insufficient, and what must you actually specify (how data is partitioned across nodes and how a request is routed to the right node, replication for availability, capacity planning, handling traffic SKEW / hot keys, and what happens when a node fails)?
shortTitle: How would you scale a key-value store toward ~1M requests/sec

s1_definition.profdef: Scaling a key-value store toward a million requests per second is a distributed-systems design problem, not a matter of simply adding servers, because extra servers only help if you precisely specify how data is partitioned across nodes, how a request is routed to the node that owns its key, how data is replicated for availability and read scaling, how capacity is planned from a throughput and latency budget, how traffic skew and hot keys are handled so one key does not overwhelm one node, and how the system behaves and recovers when a node fails. A complete answer defines each of these mechanisms concretely; "add more servers" is insufficient because without partitioning and routing the extra servers hold no data and receive no traffic, and hot keys and failures are not addressed by raw server count.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India must serve a million customer lookups a second. Just hiring more clerks does nothing if every customer still forms one queue at one desk; you must first decide how to split customers across desks, how each customer knows which desk is theirs, keep spare copies of each customer's file at other desks so service continues if a desk closes, work out how many desks you actually need from the expected crowd, and have a special plan for a celebrity customer whose desk gets mobbed. Only when all of that is specified do extra desks genuinely add capacity.
s1_definition.oneliner: Reaching a million requests per second means specifying partitioning, request routing, replication, capacity planning, hot-key handling, and node-failure behaviour, because adding servers alone does nothing until data is partitioned and requests are routed to the node that owns each key.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Scaling a key-value store toward a million requests per second is a distributed-systems design problem, not a matter of simply adding servers, because extra servers only help if you precisely specify how data is partitioned across nodes, how a request is routed to the node that owns its key, how data is replicated for availability and read scaling, how capacity is planned from a throughput and latency budget, how traffic skew and hot keys are handled so one key does not overwhelm one node, and how the system behaves and recovers when a node fails. A complete answer defines each of these mechanisms concretely; "add more servers" is insufficient because without partitioning and routing the extra servers hold no data and receive no traffic, and hot keys and failures are not addressed by raw server count.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine National Bank of India must serve a million customer lookups a second. Just hiring more clerks does nothing if every customer still forms one queue at one desk; you must first decide how to split customers across desks, how each customer knows which desk is theirs, keep spare copies of each customer's file at other desks so service continues if a desk closes, work out how many desks you actually need from the expected crowd, and have a special plan for a celebrity customer whose desk gets mobbed. Only when all of that is specified do extra desks genuinely add capacity.

**One line to remember:** Reaching a million requests per second means specifying partitioning, request routing, replication, capacity planning, hot-key handling, and node-failure behaviour, because adding servers alone does nothing until data is partitioned and requests are routed to the node that owns each key.

sections.s2_technical:
The reason "add more servers" is insufficient is the crux. A key-value store's capacity comes from spreading both data and traffic across nodes, but spreading only happens if you have a partitioning scheme and a routing mechanism. If you add servers without partitioning, they simply hold no data and receive no requests, so throughput does not rise. Even with partitioning, raw server count does nothing about a single hot key whose traffic all lands on one node, and nothing about what happens when a node dies. So the real answer is to specify the mechanisms, and there are several that must each be addressed.

Partitioning decides how the keyspace is divided across nodes. You hash the key and map it to a partition, and the strong choice is consistent hashing with virtual nodes on a ring, because it spreads keys evenly and, critically, lets you add or remove nodes while moving only about a 1/N fraction of the data rather than remapping everything as naive modulo would. Virtual nodes keep the per-node load even and let you weight bigger machines. Partitioning is what actually converts more servers into more capacity, because each node then owns and serves a distinct slice of the keyspace.

Routing decides how a request reaches the node that owns its key. There are a few models. A coordinator or proxy layer can receive every request, compute the owning node from the ring, and forward it; this is simple for clients but adds a hop. A smart client can hold the ring topology and route directly to the owning node, saving the hop at the cost of client complexity and topology distribution. Or any node can act as a coordinator and forward internally, as Dynamo-style systems do. Whatever the model, the routing must be fast, must stay consistent with the current ring as nodes join and leave, usually via gossip or a membership service, and must avoid becoming a bottleneck itself, so the routing layer is horizontally scaled or pushed into clients.

Replication provides availability and read scaling. Each key is stored on more than one node, typically the N successive nodes clockwise on the ring, so if one node fails another copy still serves the key. The replication factor, for example three, is a durability and availability choice. You also decide consistency: with quorum reads and writes, you require a write to be acknowledged by W replicas and a read to consult R replicas such that R plus W is greater than N, which guarantees a read sees the latest write while still tolerating some node failures; relaxing this gives faster but eventually consistent reads. Replication is also how reads scale, since multiple replicas can serve reads of the same key in parallel.

Capacity planning turns the target into a concrete node count. You start from the budget: a million requests per second at a target latency, with a read-to-write ratio and an average value size. If a single well-configured node sustains, say, a hundred thousand operations per second within the latency target, you need at least ten nodes just for throughput, then you multiply by the replication factor for the copies, add headroom for peak bursts above the average, account for memory to hold the working set and network bandwidth for the value sizes, and add spare capacity so the loss of a node or two does not push the rest over their limit. You plan for the peak, not the average, and you leave margin for failover load.

Handling traffic skew and hot keys is where naive designs fail even with good partitioning, because real traffic is not uniform. A single extremely popular key, like a celebrity account or a viral item, sends all its traffic to the one node that owns it, overwhelming that node regardless of cluster size. The mitigations are specific: cache the hot key in front of the store, for example in a local or distributed cache, so most reads never reach the owning node; replicate the hot key to extra nodes and spread its reads across them; for a hot counter, shard the single key into sub-keys and aggregate; and add per-key rate limiting or admission control so one key cannot starve others. Detecting hot keys through per-key metrics is a prerequisite, and the system should react, ideally automatically.

Node-failure behaviour must be explicit because at this scale failures are routine, not exceptional. When a node fails, requests for its keys are served by the surviving replicas, so with a replication factor of three the data remains available through two other copies. The ring membership is updated, typically via a gossip protocol and failure detection, so routing stops sending traffic to the dead node. The failed node's share of load redistributes to its replica peers, which is why you planned spare capacity. When the node returns or a replacement joins, it receives its portion of the data from peers through a background, throttled transfer, and techniques like hinted handoff let writes that occurred during the outage be delivered to the recovered node so it catches up. You also guard against split-brain and ensure that temporary failures do not cause data loss by relying on the quorum settings.

Senior nuances: separate the control plane, membership and topology, from the data plane so topology churn does not stall requests; use consistent hashing with virtual nodes rather than modulo so scaling and recovery move minimal data; pick quorum parameters to match the consistency the use case needs, since a balance lookup and a like counter tolerate different staleness; put a caching tier in front for read-heavy and hot-key traffic; and monitor per-node and per-key metrics so skew and failures are detected and acted on quickly. The whole point is that a million requests per second is achieved by specifying all these mechanisms together, not by any single lever.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs a key-value store for account balances and session data serving close to a million requests per second, and a manager suggested just adding servers. This is exactly the "add more servers is insufficient" case: without partitioning and routing, extra servers hold nothing and serve nothing.

Problem 2 — The store must survive node failures without losing availability. This is exactly the replication case, keeping each key on several nodes so a failure is transparent, with quorum settings tuned for the consistency balances need.

Problem 3 — One corporate account, used by a massive merchant, receives a wildly disproportionate share of reads. This is exactly the hot-key skew case, requiring caching, hot-key replication, and per-key rate limiting so that one key does not overwhelm its node.

Our mini-project demonstrates the design. The code defines a `ConsistentHashRing` with virtual nodes for partitioning, a `Router` that locates a key's primary and replica nodes, a `KvCluster` that replicates writes and serves quorum reads, a `HotKeyCache` in front for skewed traffic, and a demo that routes requests across nodes, serves a key after a node failure from a replica, and shows a hot key being absorbed by the cache plus a capacity-planning calculation.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a target of one million requests per second, a per-node ceiling, a replication factor of three, and account keys including a very hot merchant key.

Step 1: Capacity planning turns the target into a node count. Dividing the target by what one node can sustain and multiplying by a peak headroom factor gives the number of throughput nodes, and the replication factor then dictates how many copies of each key exist. This shows concretely that the cluster size comes from a budget, not a guess, which is the heart of why "add servers" is not an answer by itself.

Step 2: A write for an account key is routed by the consistent-hash ring to the key's replica set, the primary plus the next distinct nodes clockwise, and the value is stored on each live replica. The write succeeds once the write quorum of acknowledgements is met, which is how durability and availability are balanced.

Step 3: A read for the same key consults replicas until the read quorum is satisfied, returning the value. Because the read and write quorums overlap, the read is guaranteed to see the latest committed write while still tolerating a node being down.

Step 4: The node that is primary for an account key then fails. Because the key is replicated to three nodes, the read is still served from a surviving replica, so the data remains available, and in a real system gossip would mark the node down so routing stops sending it traffic and its load redistributes to peers, which is why spare capacity was planned.

Step 5: A hot merchant key is hammered with a hundred thousand reads. The cache in front serves the overwhelming majority from memory so they never reach the owning node, and a per-key rate limit sheds any excess, so only a tiny number of reads actually hit the backend. This shows that hot-key skew is solved by caching, replication of the hot key, and rate limiting, not by cluster size. The output shows the capacity plan, the quorum read, the survival of a node failure, and the cache absorbing the hot key.

```
2026-10-24 15:39:05 INFO    capacity plan: 1000000 rps / 100000 per node * 1.5 headroom = 15 nodes (RF=3)
2026-10-24 15:39:05 INFO    quorum read SAV2001 = balance=1000000
2026-10-24 15:39:05 WARNING primary of SAV2001 failed → serving from a replica (RF=3)
2026-10-24 15:39:05 INFO    after failure, read SAV2001 = balance=1000000  ← available via replica; load redistributes to peers
2026-10-24 15:39:05 INFO    hot key MERCHANT9: 100000 reads → only 1 reached backend (cache + per-key rate limit absorbed the rest)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  1,000,000 req/sec
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────────── Routing (smart client / proxy) ────────────────┐
  │ hash(key) on consistent-hash ring (vnodes) → replica set        │
  └───────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────┘
          ┌────────────────────┼───────────────────────┐
          ▼                     ▼                        ▼
   ┌──────────┐ replicate ┌──────────┐ replicate ┌──────────┐
   │ node (primary)│──────▶│ node (r2) │─────────▶│ node (r3) │  RF=3
   └──────────┘           └──────────┘           └──────────┘
     write: W=2 acks            read: R=2 (R+W>N → latest)

  ── Node failure ──
  primary → gossip marks down → reads served by r2/r3 → load → peers
            → recovered node catches up via hinted handoff (background)

  ── Hot key (skew) ──
  MERCHANT9 flood → ┌ HotKeyCache (serves most reads) ┐
                    └ per-key rate limit (sheds excess) ┘ → only ~0 reach backend
```

  ── The 6 things you MUST specify (not "add servers") ──────────
  1 Partitioning   → consistent hash + vnodes (converts nodes→capacity)
  2 Routing        → smart client / coordinator → owning node
  3 Replication    → RF=3, quorum R+W>N (availability + consistency)
  4 Capacity plan  → target/per-node * headroom * RF
  5 Hot-key skew   → cache + replicate hot key + per-key rate limit
  6 Node failure   → replicas serve, gossip down, hinted handoff recover

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────────
  1 plan nodes = ceil(1M/100K * 1.5)
  2 put(key) → ring.replicasFor → write W replicas
  3 get(key) → read R replicas (R+W>N → latest)
  4 failPrimary → replicas still serve → peers absorb load
  5 hot key → cache.get absorbs; rate limit sheds excess

sections.s6_takeaway:
Scaling a key-value store toward a million requests per second is a distributed-systems design problem, and the first thing I say is why "add more servers" is not an answer. A store's capacity only grows if both data and traffic are spread across nodes, and that spreading happens only if you have a partitioning scheme and a routing mechanism. Add servers without partitioning and they hold no data and receive no requests, so throughput does not move, and raw server count does nothing about a single hot key whose traffic all lands on one node, or about what happens when a node dies. So the real answer is to specify the mechanisms, and there are six I walk through.

Partitioning decides how the keyspace is divided, and I use consistent hashing with virtual nodes on a ring, because it spreads keys evenly and lets me add or remove nodes while moving only about a 1/N fraction of the data instead of remapping everything like naive modulo, with virtual nodes keeping the per-node load even and letting me weight bigger machines. Routing decides how a request reaches the node that owns its key, either through a coordinator or proxy that forwards, or a smart client that holds the ring and routes directly, and it must stay consistent with the current topology through gossip and must not become a bottleneck itself. Replication provides availability and read scaling by storing each key on the next several nodes clockwise, say a replication factor of three, and I tune consistency with quorums, requiring W replicas to acknowledge a write and R replicas for a read such that R plus W is greater than N, so a read sees the latest write while tolerating failures.

Capacity planning turns the target into a node count from a budget: a million requests per second divided by what one tuned node sustains at the target latency gives the throughput nodes, I multiply by the replication factor for the copies, add headroom because I plan for the peak and not the average, and leave spare capacity so losing a node does not push the rest over their limit. Handling traffic skew and hot keys is where naive designs fail even with good partitioning, because one extremely popular key sends all its traffic to one node regardless of cluster size, so I put a cache in front to absorb most reads, replicate the hot key to extra nodes, shard a hot counter into sub-keys, and add per-key rate limiting, all driven by per-key metrics to detect the skew. Node-failure behaviour must be explicit because at this scale failures are routine: when a node fails the surviving replicas still serve its keys, gossip marks it down so routing stops sending it traffic, its load redistributes to the peers I planned spare capacity for, and when it recovers it catches up through a throttled background transfer with hinted handoff delivering the writes it missed.

On my project at National Bank of India we built exactly this kind of store for balances and sessions, and when a manager suggested simply adding servers I had to explain that without partitioning and routing those servers do nothing. We used consistent hashing with virtual nodes, a replication factor of three with quorum reads and writes, planned the node count from a throughput and latency budget with headroom, and the lesson that stuck most was the hot key: one huge merchant account would have melted its node until we fronted it with a cache and per-key rate limiting, after which almost none of its reads reached the backend. The nuances I add are to separate the control plane of membership and topology from the data plane so topology churn does not stall requests, to pick quorum parameters to match the consistency each use case needs since a balance and a like counter tolerate different staleness, and to monitor per-node and per-key metrics so skew and failures are caught and acted on fast.

The one-line summary I give an interviewer is that reaching a million requests per second means concretely specifying partitioning with consistent hashing, routing to the owning node, replication with quorums for availability and consistency, capacity planning from a latency and throughput budget with headroom, hot-key handling through caching and rate limiting, and node-failure behaviour where replicas keep serving and recovery is background and throttled, because adding servers alone does nothing until data is partitioned and requests are routed.

---

keyPoints: Horizontal scaling: add more instances behind load balancer
Vertical scaling: bigger machine — has limits
Auto-scaling: based on CPU, memory, request rate metrics
Sharding: partition data across databases for write scalability
